full_judgment:
4. It is the case of the plaintiff that suit land which originally belonged to Ananda Charan Datta and Ghana Charan Datta, was put into auction for arrear rents in Rent Case No. 154 of 1946 and pursuant to the decree one, Abdul Latif Chowdhury, son of Haji Mobarak Ali of village Saga char under Patia Upazilla purchased the suit land in Rent Execution Case No.131 of 1947 on 8-4-1948 and sale was confirmed on 11-5-1948 and possessing the suit land until he executed power-of-attorney on 18-4-1968 in favour of his son, Abdul Basher Chowdhury and close well-wisher, Abdul Jalil and power-of-attorney holders mutated their names and also paid rents regularly. In PS survey the suit land although recorded wrongly in the name, of Nasiruddin, Hosne Ara Begum, Khadija Begum and Captain Bakhtiar but recorded persons never possessed the suit land in BS Survey, to the knowledge of the aforesaid persons and also of the Government. Defendant Nos.5 and 6.recorded the suit land in the name of Abdul Latif. The aforesaid power-of-attorney holders by registered deed dated 6-1-1985 and 21-1-1986 transferred the suit land in favour of plaintiff No.3. which was registered in the Sub Registry office, Pahartalli; by these two deeds 20 acres of land was gifted in favour of plaintiff Nos. l and 2 who got possession. After getting the, suit land as aforesaid, plaintiffs demarcated the suit land having title and possession and paid rents regularly. Plaintiffs also cut earth from the suit land, filled the lower portion and developed the suit land and constructed home-stead. Plaintiffs possessed the null land through borgaders, wherein defendants or anybody else had no possession or title and they could not demand the suit land and by this possession, plaintiffs acquired title by adverse possession. Plaintiff possessed the suit land peacefully but at present, defendant Nos.l-4 in different ways disturbed the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs and they want to include the shares in their proposed housing society and the said persons with the government employees continuously giving threat. Plaintiffs turned down the proposal of the aforesaid persons where-upon interested persons became furious and on 14-6-1987 with some gunda elements tried to get into possession by force and thereby tried to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land. Plaintiffs husband and plaintiff's tenants and local people intervened and the gunda elements leave the suit land giving open threat that they will get the suit land from government, defendant Nos. 5 and 6, through Magistrate and Police they will come back and dispossess the plaintiff. Plaintiff with her husband went to defendant No.7, Tahsildar for inquiry but did not get any information. But the plaintiff could see some employees of defendant No.5 conspiring with the gunda elements for satisfying their lust. Defendant Nos.5 and 6 only can realize tax from the plaintiff, hence the suit. 

 6. Defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the written statement after taking preliminary objections as to maintainability of the suit, denied the plaint case line by line. It is their specific case that suit land originally belonged to Ananda Charan Datta and Gyananda Charan Datta and Nilmani Datta. 45.96 acres of land was recorded as projabili in the RS khatian. The entire land of jote for arrear of rent was put into auction and government purchased the suit land on 18-3-1934 and for managing the auction purchased land for which defendants' instituted further suit. The said lands purchased after auction still remain in previous Jote No.140. After 14 jote created by resettlement of the suit land in Miscellaneous Case No.651 of 1945-46 the suit land was resettled. After resettlement, Brojalal Chose, Sumon Lal Chose got 15.48 acres of land from several R.S. dag numbers involved in the suit and Jote No.180 was created which was recorded in R.S. No. 836/16. Brojalal Chose sold his land of Jote Nos.180. 181. 182 to Nasir Uddin, Khadija Begurn and Harun Matin and also to other persons and thereby became title less. The aforesaid purchasers in Mutation Case No.47/52-53 and JM Case No. 114/54-55 recorded their names in Jotekhatian No.835/16 and according to their possession, the suit land has been recorded in SA khatian Nos.74 and 94. The aforesaid purchase is, Nasiruddin, Khadija Begum and Harun Matin were non-Bengali and left the country for Pakistan during war of liberation and never came back and Government as per PO No. 16 of 1972 declared the property as enemy property. The said property during BS survey was recorded in the name of Government of Bangladesh. To protect the said property from illegal trespassers or illegal strangers in 1975 Government appointed Md Nurul Huda (defendant No.3) as care taker. Government through Miscellaneous Cases Nos.6 of 1980-81, 7 of 1980-81, 8 of 1980-81, 9 of 1980-81, 2 of 1981 -82 leased out the property in favour of Md Solaiman, Faruq Ahmed and others. Brojalal Ghosh was never tenant either under Ananda Charan or Gyananda Charan and was never resettlement holder of Government. Brojalal Ghose, Benulal Ghose and their heirs, who were owners of jote No. 180, 181, 182 through Resettlement Case No. 651/45-46, sold the suit land to Nash Uddin, Khodeja Begum, Harun Malin and others by several kabalas. The case of the plaintiffs of mutation of their names in Mutation Case No. 384/78-79, 480/78-79 is totally false and no such khatian was opened in the office of Assistant Commissioner, Land and Mutation Case No. 401/78-79 was not related to the suit property; that mutation case was related to Nurul Alam, son of Ashraf Ali, of village: Bakalia, Chittagong in respect of 0.28 decimals of land and Mutation Case No.430/78-79 was in respect of Pear Mohammad of Sakir-51, Keranigonj, Police Station Kotwali, Chittagong for 0.57 decimals of land. The aforesaid mutation case and khatian of the plaintiffs are false and prepared for ulterior motive. Plaintiffs and husband of plaintiff, Abul Bashar are members of gang of forged deed and they created several forged deeds and after creating different forged deeds they wanted to grab the property illegally. Criminal cases have been instituted against Abul Bashar, husband of plaintiff and also against Md Abdul Jalil and others. Double Mouring Police Station Case No. 32(1)87 under section 467/468/109 of the Penal Code was initiated on 30-1-1987. Charge-sheet was submitted and charge was framed and the case is pending in Criminal Motion No. 381 of 1989 which is pending before the Additional District Judge, 1st court, Chittagong. On these grounds defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 7. In the suit, plaintiff examined one witness and he was particularly cross examined by the Government. Government did not adduce any witness nor exhibited any documents. 

 8. Learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong by judgment and decree dated 30-4-1995 decreed the suit on the finding that "defendant government did not take any step to prove the case by adducing any witness or exhibiting any documents'. Learned Judge thereafter took into consideration as regard possession of the plaintiff which is the crux for deciding case of permanent injunction. On consideration of exhibits 3 series, exhibits 2 series, exhibits 4 series, exhibits 7 series, exhibits 5 series and exhibits 6 series held by the aforesaid exhibits, plaintiff has been able to prove their possession of the suit property and decreed the suit. 

 9. Against this decision defendant-Government preferred Other Appeal No. 248 of 1998 out of time by 1230 days. The application for condonation of delay was filed. After contesting hearing the delay was condoned. 

 11. Mr Serajul Haque with Mr Md Bashuddin Zindigir, learned advocates appearing for the petitioner. For the non contesting defendant No.3 of the suit, Mr Fida M 'Carnal, Mr AJ Mohammad All and Mr Ahsanul Karim, learned Advocates along with bunch of lawyers appeared. Mr Md Jaber, learned Assistant Attorney-General with some government pleaders appeared for defendant No. 1, appellant, opposite party No. 1. All the lawyers appeared in this rule whit 1 is for condonation of delay, not a rule on decree but made argument one after another tirelessly which cover all categories of cases on this rule. 

 12. Mr. Serajul Haque, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that, delay was 1230 days but in the application for condo-nation of delay no explanation was given nor the learned Judge ever considered whether the applicant gave any reason far less sufficient or satisfactory for condonation of delay and in one sentence, only in one sentence this long delay has been condoned on taking into consideration of the findings of other suit filed by the plaintiffs affirmed up to the Appellate Division and submits that, since delay has not been properly explained the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge being devoid of any substance is liable to be set-aside. Learned Advocate in the course of argument referred to Civil Revision No.701 of 2005 arisen from the selfsame order of the learned District Judge passed in Other Appeal No.255 of 1999 arisen from the selfsame suit against the selfsame judgment of the trial court wherein learned District Judge on condoning the delay of 1569 days, admitted the appeal for hearing and this judgment was challenged in Civil Revision No.701 of 2005; the High Court Division made the rule absolute and dismissed Other Appeal No.255 of 1999. Against which, defendant government did not proceed further, Learned Advocate further submits that against the selfsame judgment two appeals cannot be filed by same defendant and since Judgment passed by the High Court Division dismissing Other Appeal No.255 of 1999 against which government did not proceed further the decision operates as resjudicata on the facts of the given case. Learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the decisions of Province of East Pakistan vs Meajan Ali Ahmed and 15 others, 18 DLR (SC) 343, the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and Assistant Custodian, Vested property, Sirajganj vs Md Abdul Majid, 2 BLC (AD) 11 and the case of The Principal Secretary, President's Secretariat, vs Mohammad Abdul Batten, 1994 BLT (AD) 90. In the decision of 1994 BLT (AD) 90 Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court did not condone the delay of 195 days and observed that: 

 "(2) This petition is barred by limitation of 195 days. There is an application for con-donation of the delay. Grounds taken for condonation are that the relevant Ministry asked for legal opinion on 9-9-93 for filing a Leave petition and also to get a certified copy of the High Court Division's order, that the File was sent to the Attorney-General and then to the Additional Attorney-General for opinion, that, thereafter, it was sent to the Solicitor "who was pleased to appoint an Advocate-on-Record", that the Solicitor's Office asked the Ministry of Home Affairs for supplying necessary documents and papers, that thereafter, necessary fund was ought for etc. These are not at all good grounds for condonation of the delay; rather these show utter negligence, carelessness, inefficiency or, may be, connivance of persons/officials of the petitioner-government who handled this matter. When an Assistant Attorney-General (Mr. Mashuque Hossain Ahmed) had appeared before the High Court Division and argued on behalf of the Government he certainly knew of the result of the writ petition. As such certified copy of the impugned order could have been easily obtained in time, the writ petition was filed four years after the impugned order of dismissal of the respondent under MLR 9. No Affidavit was filed raising questions as to its maintainability and inordinate delay. As to the delay in filing this Leave petition, whether it was either deliberate or due to utter negligence on the part of the petitioner's officers, there is no good ground for its condonation." 

 "4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury has had no difficulty in showing that on these facts, there had been delay which it is entirely impossible to excuse. The government were aware from the outset that on account of the floods in Bogra they were already out of time on the day when the Deputy commissioner made his reference, i.e. the 22nd October, 1962. The case arising as it did out of the acquisition of rent receiving interests, a subject which has given rise to intensive litigation, of which in the main the Board of Revenue was presumably in charge, it is not easy to see why in this particular case, affecting, as is said one of the biggest Hats in the Province and a major source of revenue for the district of Bogra, it should have been necessary to relegate the papers after the decision of the High Court to the district authorities for their opinion, which in the circumstances could hardly have possessed any value. The Government's case rested on statutes, and not on considerations of balance or of justice in regard to local conditions. Before the High Court, the Province was represented by a Government Pleader. This was a case which should certainly have been dealt with in Dacca without need of reference to Bogra at all, but even allowing for the unnecessary reference to the district authorities, and the pre-occupation of those authorities with the flood, there are delays following after the 22nd October, 1962 which cannot be explained on any ground that can be acceptable in a Court to avoid the effect of limitation in respect of right that have become vested through lapse of time. There was no need for the Board of Revenue to have taken 16 'days' before referring the matter to the Legal Remembrancer, or for the Legal Remembrancer to take another 5 days before referring the matter to the Government Pleader. Worst of all is the delay of some 45 days between obtaining copies of the judgment and decree and the filing of the petition for special leave. There is no excuse for that particular period, when the file was not passing between offices, but was conceivably in the possession of the Government Pleader, who had already given an opinion in favour of filing an appeal. Once time limited by law has expired, the party which is out of time must, particularly in a case where vested rights have been assured through lapse of time, that here it is difficult to find an explanation for any period of the delay which has been allowed to occur,totaling 113 days in all, that is, nearly twice the prescribed period of limitation. 5. We are satisfied that this is a case in which the prayer for condonation cannot be entertained. The order of condonation made at the time when leave was granted was passed ex parte and is rested moreover, on an application which gave the impression that the entire period of delay was due to the floods in Bogra. Now that the true facts are known it is clear that there is no ground for allowing condonation. There is reason to think that there are other modes in which uniformity in the application of the Ordinance of 1960 can be restored qua this particular Hat." 

 16. Mr Md Jaber, learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing for the opposite party, on the other hand submits that, judgment passed by the learned District Judge being well reasonable is maintainable. Learned Assistant Attorney General further submits that in the application for condonation of delay, 1230 days was not properly explained but government filed supplementary-affidavit and also application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure explaining the delay and reasons stated therein being satisfactory, learned District Judge acted within his jurisdiction in applying his discretion by condoning the delay. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that in Title Suit No.97 of 1994 decree was passed for the plaintiff in respect of the self-same land but in Appeal from Original Decree No.131 of 1998 High Court Division found that plaintiff by applying gigantic fraud tried to grab the suit property by showing a dead man alive in auction proceeding of 1948 and set-aside the decree and sent the suit back on remand. Against this decision, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was taken properly to the Appellate Division and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1476 of 2008 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1477 of 2008, both these civil petitions for leave to appeal were dismissed as not being pressed showing that plaintiffs of that suit and also of this suit played fraud upon the court and fraud having been detected vitiated everything. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on reference to a voluminous counter-affidavit, submits that this property cannot be a secular property as Government of Bangladesh purchased the suit property on 18-3-1943 in execution of a decree in respect of the suit land, as such, whatever title plaintiff has, extinguished after the sale has been confirmed. Learned Advocate further submits that plaintiff has no locus standi to file any suit on the subject matter. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits, that, in condoning the delay fate of appeal has not reached its finality and it is only admission by which parties now can contest the suit over the dispute as such plaintiff should not be prejudiced in admission of appeal. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on reference to voluminous counter-affidavit with some papers and "Shampurak Abedan" and also application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, submits that, if the application for condonation of delay be considered along with `Shampurak Abedan Patra" and the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, then sufficient reason can be found for condoning the delay. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that from Title Suit No.79 of 1994 it appears that suit was filed for declaration of title, confirmation of possession with some other reliefs and from that suit, present plaintiff herself strike out her name and filed the instant suit for permanent injunction. Since plaintiff strike out her name from Title Suit No.97 of 1994, she has no locus standi to file the instant suit as relief sought for in the earlier suit have total impact on the instant suit. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that it is admitted position that certain portion of the schedule property is abandoned property, as such as per provision of Article 14 of PO 16 of 1972 this suit cannot proceed. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that unless delay be condoned, the questions relating to the maintainability of the suit shall remain unanswered. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on submission of condonation of delay relied on the decisions of Director of Housing and Settlement vs Abdul Majid Howlader, 9 BLC (AD) 51 wherein it is held:— 

 "16. There has been delay of 542 days in filing the revisional application by the appellant. The High Court Division refused to condone the delay on the ground that the petitioner before the High Court Division was negligent in taking step in filing the revisional application against the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 118 of 1997 affirming the decree passed in Title Suit No. 191 of 1996. In the background of the provision of law the suit filed by the respondents and decreed by the courts below was being totally non-entertainable by the civil Court the High Court Division was required to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct the gross error of law committed by the courts below. In that view of the matter we are of the view that the High Court Division was not correct in refusing to condone the delay and consequent thereupon in not entertaining the revisional application. The High Court Division was quite unmindful of the fact that the reliefs granted in the suit were not legally available to the respondents and consequently allowing the gross error of law to remain in effect that would amount to allow the respondents to enjoy the fruit of the decree although under the law they are not entitled to the same and thus if the decree so passed in favour of the respondents remains winter feed the appellant and respondent No. 20 would be deprived of their legal claim in the property in suit. Since the respondents obtained a decree from a Court which was not competent to pass the same being barred by the law to entertain the suit of the kind filed by the respondents or, in other words, in view of the provision of law barring the civil Court from entertaining the kind of the suit filed by the plaintiffs and decreeing the same, the High court Division was required to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct the gross error of law committed by the courts below. The High Court Division in spite of filing of revisional application beyond the period prescribed by a long standing practice is quite competent in its revisional jurisdiction to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct gross error of law committed by the courts below or, in other words, to put law straight in a case like the present one and in that view of the matter we are of the view High Court Division was not correct in not entertaining the revisional application upon condonation of the delay for which explanation was offered, though not accepted by the said Division on the view that the petitioner was guilty of serious negligence and lathes. Such explanation for condonation of inordinate delay of 542 days, cannot be accepted as satisfactory ". But the fact remains that the decree that was passed by the courts below and as against which revisional application was filed was a nullity because the civil court entertained the suit in spite of the provision of law barring the same from entertaining the suit either questioning the order passed or action taken in a proceeding initiated under the Act for acquisition of a property, as in the case of the property in suit, and that because of the fact that upon acquisition the property in suit vested in the Government and for that the respondents were not entitled to have a decree from a civil Court to have the acquired property released in their favour. Since the suit of the respondents itself was not entertain able by the civil Court, as such,the decree so passed in the suit being a nullity, in our view, no useful purpose would be served in sending the revisional application upon allowing the appeal, to the High Court Division to entertain the same for disposal finally and thereby prolonging the litigation. In that view of the matter we are inclined to dispose of the matter once and for all." 

 "5. As it appears, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that admittedly the suit land was acquired by the government for rehabilitation of the refugees who migrated to then East Pakistan from India. The suit land was allotted to Rustom Ali. Admittedly Rustom Ali, after getting allotment of the suit land, did not construct any homestead on the same and allowed defendant No. 4 to possess the suit land on the strength of an agreement, Exhibit-2, in contravention of terms and conditions of the allotment, inasmuch as clause 5 of the letter of allotment, which has been marked as Exhibit-A3, provides that the allottees must maintain the houses at their own expenses whenever necessary and they may construct additional sheds according to their requirement within their compound at their own cost with previous permission of the collector but the refugees will have no right to sell or otherwise dispose of the land and buildings; however, if any refugee migrated at any time he will have to take over the land and buildings to the Collector who will dispose those on the advice of the government; thus Exhibit A3 shows that Rustom Ali had no right to make any transfer or sell the suit land infavour of Abdul Jabbar as admittedly, Rustom Ali did not execute any sale deed in favour of Abdul Jabbar and the very claim of the plaintiff is that Abdul Jabbar, on the strength of a contract, entered into possession of the suit land and sold the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by kabala deed dated 11-12-1983 though admittedly Abdul Jabbar did not acquire any title in the suit land on the basis of the agreement dated 25-12-1987 and so by kabala deed dated 11-12-1983, plaintiff did not acquire any title in the suit land; further, admittedly the government did not enter into any contract with the plaintiff and did not hand over possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff and accordingly the plaintiff is nothing but a trespasser upon the suit land on the strength of Exhibits 1 and 2; further in terms of section 5 of East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXIV of 1970 the Deputy Commissioner, Jessore, with a view to get recovery of possession of the suit land from the plaintiff and other unauthorized occupants, duly issued a notice which has been marked as Exhibit A5 and the plaintiff, although gave an undertaking by writing to hand over possession of the suit land in favour of the defendant, filed the suit and got a temporary injunction restraining the government from taking over possession of the suit land; further the plaintiff, being an unauthorized occupant in the suit land, had also no locus standi to maintain a suit for permanent injunction against the defendants who in exercise of the power under section 5 of the Ordinance XXIV of 1970 duly issued notice and neither the learned Assistant Judge nor the learned Additional District Judge considered this aspect of the matter; it is the settled principle of law that a trespasser cannot maintain a suit for permanent injunction against a rightful owner; both the Courts below misread the provisions of Article 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, inasmuch as the plaintiff, being a trespasser, cannot get protection of law to retain her illegal possession in the suit land; the notice of eviction was served upon the plaintiff on 19-1-1986 whereupon plaintiff undertook to hand over the possession of the suit land on 1-2-1986 but instead, filed the instant suit on 4-2-1986 and after filing of the suit that she on 28-1-1987, got Exhibit 3 which is hit by the principle of his pendens as provided in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act; moreover, defendant No. 1, after taking preliminary steps for eviction of the plaintiff, issued notice vide Exhibit -A5. for eviction, of an unauthorized occupant from government land and the right of the Government to evict the defendant cannot be defeated by creating a subsequent kabala from Rustom Ali whose allotment deed had already been cancelled by order dated 7-12-1986 and after the above cancellation, Rustom Ali had no right to execute and register any kabala in favour of the plaintiff." 

 "7. Now, the question posed by Mr Ali is whether the High Court which recorded the impugned order was competent to alter the said order in exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. He argued that even if it be assumed that the order dated 31-4-70 amounted to an order of abatement as contended by Mr Moinul Huq, there is no escape from the finding that the said order was passed on the basis of a false affidavit and a false certificate of death. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, even if there were an alternative remedy, it would not bar the exercise of power under section 151 of the Code by the Court. Section 151 preserves the inherent power of the court to make such order as may be necessary for the ends of justice. It may be noted that the provisions of the Code are generally meant to serve the ends of justice but in their very nature they cannot read all possible circumstances. Consequently every court has an inherent power to make any order it considers necessary for the ends of justice. Reference on this point may be made to the following cases, namely: 19 CWN 419 (Peary Choudhury vs Sence Dass) 45. 151 (Debi Baksh Singh vs Habib Shah) 45, CWN 392 (Akira Bibivs Mohammad Ali) AIR 1934 Allahabad 287 (Lachhman Rai vs Jang Bahadur Rai), AIR 1937 Sind 101 (Mohanlal vs Khushalibai) (1958) 10 DLR 79 PLD 1958 Dae. 295 (Ganesh Chandra Basu vs Bashu Laskar). What has been held in the above cases is that the court has an inherent power under section 151 of the Code to set-aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the Court has also power under the aforesaid section 151 of the Code to vacate an order obtained by misleading the Court and practicing fraud upon it. In the present case the High Court recorded an order that the appeal had been abated in view of an affidavit and a deal certificate which were latter found to be false. The court was evidently misled in recording the order as regards abatement though there was no basis for the same. The said order had, therefore, no legal effect. This will appear from the observation of the High Court. It is as follows: 

 "4. Details of the history as the right to the rent of the ex-rent receiver on the acquisition the rent receiving interest need not be set out in detail, excepting that when the rent suit was filed in 1960 the law as to right of ex-rent receiver recover arrear rent is to be found in section 63C of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which, inter alia, provides that all arrears of rent and cess together with interest thereon which remained due to any rent receiver in respect of an interest on the date of acquisition, and which have not become barred limitation shall continue to be recoverable by such rent receiver amicably through Civil Court, from the persons liable to pay them. We have referred only to the relevant part bereft of irrelevant parts. This provision of law has no doubt preserved the right of ex-rent receiver to realize his dues as rent from his tenants and this right is therefore to be construed in the light of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Under section 3 of the with the notification made in the Official Gazette all rent receiving interests of the rent receiver shall vest in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. It is not disputed that on and from 14th April, 1956 rent receiving interest of all rent receivers in Bangladesh were acquired under this section, and so the relationship of "landlord and tenant so far as the previous rent receivers have ceased to exists. The suit could be filed as money suit and the decree holder in any suit whether described as money suit or rent suit has ceased to have his right treat it as rent suit under the Bengal Tenancy Act." 

 "7. Mr TH Khan , counsel for the appellant, contended that since the properties in question, though mortgaged with the appellants being abandoned property, the decree obtained by the respondent Bank is incapable of execution in view of the fact that the decretal abandoned properties have vested in the Government. There is also the express bar in the provisions of Article 14 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Management, control and Disposal) Order, 1972, PO No. 16 of 1972. The trial court as well as the High Court Division ought to have taken judicial notice of such provisions in spite of the government's failure to invoke them , Article 14 provides as follows; 

 "14. (1) Any property vested in the government under this Order shall be exempt from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority, and no injunction or other order of whatever kind in respect of such property shall be granted or made by any Court or any other authority, and the Government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property by operation of any law for the time being in force. 

 (2) Any such legal process as aforesaid subsisting immediately before the commencement of this Order shall cease to have effect on such commencement and all abandoned properties in custody of any Court, receiver, guardian or other person or persons appointed by it, shall upon delivery of the same being called for by the government, be delivered to the Government." 

 From these provisions it appears that once any property is declared or treated as abandoned property under the aforesaid Act it cannot be subjected to any legal process such as seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority and further, that the government cannot be divested or dispossessed of such properties. 

 12. As against these circumstances which prevented the appellants from taking any steps earlier, the respondent Bank has not been able to prove that the appellants were aware of the institution of Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 or the Ex-parte decree passed by the Court or even the proceeding in execution in title Execution No. 46 of 1980 until the advertisement appeared in the newspaper already referred to above. The respondent Bank equally failed to show how the decree obtained in the aforesaid suit can be executed in respect of properties which had vested in the Government under the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972. Further, though M/s. Gannysons Ltd. was made defendant No. 1 in the aforesaid title suit it was shown as having been in control and management of the government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and no relief was sought for against the company managed by the original directors. Only three Directors, namely, Dada Abdul Gani, Mad. Yunus Abdus Sattar and Abdur Rahman Abdul Majid were made proforma-defendants in the suit showing them as Directors of M/s. Gannysons Ltd. of 35-36, Bangabandhu Avenue, Dhaka. As a matter of fact, Dada Abdul Gani and Mr Yunus Abdus Sattar ceased to be directors share-holders prior to 1969. It is however, not understood why in the decree itself the proforma-defendants have been shown as "defendants". 

 13. It is also difficult to understand why, if the loan was obtained by M/s. Gannysons Ltd. before it was treated as abandoned properties, the Bank, instead of proceeding against the directors of the company who continued till it was declared as abandoned, it proceeded against it when it came to be treated as abandoned property by the Government. The Bank wanted to proceed against the properties which were offered as security against the loan obtained by the appellants before it was treated as abandoned property, but in all fairness the Bank should have made them parties as well as the Government and should have sought relief against them, particularly when the previous directors were persistently pursuing their remedies, for the release of the properties in question." 

 "16. Having given our most anxious consideration to the submissions of both sides we cannot but hold that the two Courts below have sorely missed the yard-stick with which to determine whether a property is an abandoned property or not. A property is an Abandoned Property if it falls within the definition of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In this particular case the owner himself is not coming forward to assert that he was present in Bangladesh all along. In the case relief upon by the High Court Division namely, M/s Khan Brothers Ltd. vs Government of Bangladesh 27 DLR 423, an artificial person namely a private limited company itself challenged a Gazette Notification taking over the management of its properties and assets under Articles 4 and 5 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In the other case relied upon by the High Court Division, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs M/s Speedbier Navigation Co. 30 DLR (SC) 101, five Bangladeshi partners of the firm representing 75% interest of the firm challenged the Notifications taking over their properties for management. In the last case filed upon by the High Court Division, Bangladesh vs Messrs ATI Industries Ltd. 28 DLR (AD) 120, it is the share-holders who challenged the taking over of the management of the properties of a private limited company. In the present case the real owner being totally absent from the legal proceedings instituted against him since 1972 and having not made any representation to the Government for restoration of his property the onus on the Government to prove that the owner was not present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were not known or he has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, is a negative one, meaning thereby that the government do not have to adduce positive evidence of those facts. A mere assertion will do in the facts and circumstances of the case which the appellant through PW 1 Md Syed Kamal Ali has done. The auction-purchasers witnesses, on the other hand, have only orally asserted that Dr Shamim was a Bangali, that he was present in Bangladesh throughout and that he was present in Bangladesh even in 1988. No certificate has been produced to show that he was a Bangladeshi National. No evidence has been given that Dr Shamim was in possession of the suit property on or before 28-2-72. No address of Dr Shamim has been given to prove that his whereabouts were known. There is no assertion by any of these witnesses that Dr Shamim occupied, supervised or managed in person his property. On the contrary, it is these witnesses themselves who admitted that Radio Bangladesh was in possession of the suit property since the liberation of Bangladesh. The High court Division unnecessarily shifted the onus on the appellant to prove that it required about the whereabouts of Dr. Shamim which was not at all the business of the appellant. If Dr Shamim was a Bangali and was present in Bangladesh, he may not have occupied, managed or super-vised the suit property in person for many reasons, but there is no earthly reason why he did not contest the money suit filed by Rupali Bank, why he did not resist the auction sale of his valuable suit property and why, finding Radio Bangladesh to be in possession of his property, he did not make any effort to release his property from the possession of the government. Man may lie, but circumstances do not and in the circumstances of the case it appears to us that both the courts below turned a blind eye to the admitted circumstances of the case and were swayed by the verbal assertions of the auction-purchaser's witnesses without weighing them with the attendant circumstance of the case and without probing the evidentiary value of their statements when the circumstances themselves speak volume against their assertions." 19. This Division has held in the case of Gannyson vs Sonali Bank, 36 DLR (AD) 146, that once property vests in the Government under proceedings can be taken against such property. The money decree obtained by Rupali Bank against Dr Shamim, the execution thereof and the auction sale of the suit property are all void and will not divest the Government of its title to the suit property and the auction-purchaser has acquired no title to the same by his auction purchase."
